To determine whether this reflected NfL biology or the NEFL aptamer, we used serum NfL measured by immunoassay in 740 patients from the same cohort. In the 241 patients with both measurements at the same visit, the aptamer agreed poorly with the immunoassay (r = 0.08), and within-patient change on the two platforms was uncorrelated (r = -0.02; Fig. 7B; Table S13).

Measured by immunoassay, baseline serum NfL strongly predicted the subsequent rate of decline (n = 608, r = -0.57, p = 6 x 10 -53 ), independently of baseline ALSFRS-R score.

Patients in the lowest, middle, and highest thirds of baseline NfL (median 23, 47, and 91 pg/mL) lost 4.7, 8.1, and 12.0 ALSFRS-R points per year, respectively (Kruskal-Wallis p = 2 x 10 -41 ; Fig. 7C). In contrast, within-patient change in NfL was only weakly related to the rate of decline in the 462 patients with two or more NfL measurements (r = -0.08, p = 0.08), and remained weak after correction for the reliability of the slope estimates (r = -0.15; Fig. 7D).

When patients were grouped by baseline NfL, change in NfL tracked decline in the lowest third (r = -0.32, p = 6 x 10 -5 ) and middle third (r = -0.21, p = 0.01), but not in the highest (r = 0.08, p = 0.34; Fig. 7E). Grouping on a single baseline measurement can produce this pattern through regression to the mean, so we re-estimated NfL slopes from follow-up samples alone in the 275 patients with three or more samples. Change in NfL still tracked decline in the lowest third (r = -0.23, p = 0.02) but not in the middle or highest thirds (highest r = 0.08, p = 0.51), and the difference between the lowest and highest thirds persisted (p = 0.04; Fig. S8).

A single baseline NfL measurement therefore predicts how quickly a patient will decline, whereas change in NfL tracked decline only in patients whose NfL was low at baseline. The absence of NEFL from the progression markers likely reflects how NfL is measured by the SomaScan aptamer in plasma and not NfL biology.

Change in the progression markers tracks decline within strata of baseline NfL

We next asked whether the progression markers carried information about decline that NfL did not. Change across the 72 progression markers was summarized for each patient as a composite score. The markers were selected in the same patients, so the composite was crossfitted, with markers selected in one half of the cohort and scored in the other. In the 229 patients with serial SomaScan and NfL measurements, change in the cross-fitted composite was strongly associated with the rate of decline (r = 0.475, p = 3 x 10 -14 ), whereas change in NfL was not (r = 0.02, p = 0.74). The difference between the two correlations was 0.48 (95% CI 0.28 to 0.67). Baseline NfL and change in NfL together explained 36% of the variance in the rate of decline, and adding the composite increased this to 45% (p = 1 x 10 -9 ).

Baseline NfL is measured at enrolment and is already used to stratify patients in clinical trials (13), so we repeated this comparison within thirds of baseline NfL (median 21, 41, and 71 pg/mL). Change in the composite tracked decline in every third (r = 0.49, 0.37, and 0.39 from the lowest to the highest). Change in NfL was weakly associated with decline in the lowest and middle thirds (r = 0.33 and 0.23) and was not associated with it in the highest (r = 0.07; Fig. 8A). The difference between the two was largest in the highest third (Δr = 0.32, p = 0.061), where patients declined fastest, and was in the same direction in the lowest (Δr = 0.17, p = 0.34) and middle thirds (Δr = 0.15, p = 0.29).

Change in the progression markers therefore tracked functional decline whether baseline NfL was low, intermediate, or high, whereas change in NfL did not.

The progression markers do not track decline in the fastest progressing patients

To test whether the progression markers tracked decline equally across patients, we divided the 229 patients into thirds by their rate of decline (median -11.7, -5.9, and -1.9 ALSFRS-R points per year). Change in the composite was associated with the rate of decline in the slowest third (0.115 composite units per ALSFRS-R point per year, 95% CI 0.053 to 0.177) but not in the fastest third (0.032, 95% CI -0.005 to 0.069, interaction p = 0.026; Fig. 8B). The cross-fitted composite showed the same difference (0.016 versus 0.078, p = 0.038), and 60 of the 72 progression markers tracked decline less closely in the fastest than in the slowest third (Fig. 8C). The difference was driven by the fastest progressors. Whether patients were divided into halves or quintiles, the coefficient in the slowest group remained between 0.06 and 0.08, whereas that in the fastest group fell from 0.022 in halves (p = 0.007 for the difference) to 0.004 in quintiles (Fig. S9A; Table S14). The fastest third had shorter follow-up than the slowest (1.2 versus 1.9 years) and included 43 of the 75 patients who died during follow-up. However, the difference persisted in patients followed for at least one year (p = 0.048), and adjusting for follow-up length reduced it by about a fifth. It also persisted after excluding protein and ALSFRS-R samples taken within six months of death (p = 0.013) and was in the same direction after excluding those taken within 12 months (p = 0.07; Fig. S9B).

In the fastest third, change in the composite did not track decline in any ALSFRS-R subdomain (r = -0.16 to 0.19), whereas in the slowest third it tracked decline in the bulbar, fine motor, and gross motor subdomains (r = 0.31 to 0.32) but not in the respiratory subdomain (r = 0.18; Fig. 8D; Table S14). It retained a weaker association with the decline in vital capacity (r = 0.24, 95% CI 0.05 to 0.42) and with the loss of body mass index (BMI; r = 0.35, 95% CI 0.06 to 0.58), similar to that in the slowest third (r = 0.24 and 0.16). Within the fastest third, tracking did not differ significantly between the 15 patients with bulbar onset and the 62 with limb or other onset (interaction p = 0.30; Table S14).

At enrolment, patients in the fastest third had a shorter symptom duration than those in the slowest (median 1.4 versus 3.3 years, FDR = 1 x 10 -6 ) and a faster rate of decline before enrolment (ΔFS 0.59 versus 0.24 points per month, FDR = 7 x 10 -9 ). They also had a higher baseline NfL (58.5 versus 24.4 pg/mL, FDR = 7 x 10 -15 ), but similar baseline ALSFRS-R scores (median 37 versus 39.5) and proportions with bulbar onset (19% versus 16%; Table S15). Nine of the 17 C9orf72 expansion carriers were in the fastest third, compared with one in the slowest although the difference was not significant (12% versus 1%, FDR = 0.10). During follow-up, the fastest third also declined faster in every ALSFRS-R subdomain and vital capacity, and more often required gastrostomy (23% versus 8%) and non-invasive ventilation (64% versus 34%; Table S15). Baseline NfL identified patients in the fastest third more accurately than ΔFS (AUC = 0.79 versus 0.72) but change in the composite still tracked decline in the highest third of baseline NfL (r = 0.44) and of ΔFS (r = 0.37).

The progression markers therefore lost track of decline in the fastest progressing patients, as did change in NfL in patients with the highest baseline NfL. The difference between the two correlations and its p-value are given above each group. (B) Change in the composite plotted against ALSFRS-R slope in the slowest, middle, and fastest thirds of patients by rate of decline. Lines and shaded bands show the linear fit and its 95% CI, and the coefficient (beta) is given with its 95% CI. (C) Tracking of each of the 72 progression markers in the slowest third plotted against that in the fastest third, each relative to tracking in all patients. Dashed lines mark tracking equal to that in all patients, and markers above the diagonal tracked decline less closely in the fastest than in the slowest third. (D) Pearson correlation of change in the composite with decline in ALSFRS-R total score, each ALSFRS-R subdomain, vital capacity, and body mass index (BMI) in the slowest (blue) and fastest (red) thirds. Points and bars show the correlation and its 95% CI.

Discussion

The Answer ALS cohort is the largest collection of longitudinal clinical data, serial biospecimens, and patient iPSC lines from individuals with ALS assembled to date (22, 23). This enabled us to ask whether the plasma proteins that change as patients with ALS decline originate from motor neurons, and to compare how their change and change in NfL track decline. We show that plasma proteins that distinguish patients from controls are dominated by muscle proteins leaking from damaged fibers, whereas those whose change tracks the rate of decline are secreted or shed proteins found across many tissues. Both sets replicated in an independent cohort, and a motor neuron expression map built from the same patients showed that motor neuron expression does not predict whether a plasma protein tracks decline.

Baseline serum NfL predicts how quickly patients decline but its change does not track decline, whereas change in the progression markers does so within every stratum of baseline NfL. Neither tracks decline in the fastest progressing patients.

The muscle-dominated differences between patients and controls are in line with recent large plasma proteomic studies. On SomaScan, Dergai et al. reported the largest increases in PDLIM3, TNNT2, and MYL11 and the largest decreases in ANTXR2 and ART3, with CLEC3B among their progression markers and a fall in MSTN (16). Muscle proteins were also prominent on Olink in patients and pre-symptomatic samples (15, 34). Our study extends these findings by showing that the proteins whose within-patient change tracks decline are largely distinct from those that best distinguish patients from controls, and by testing directly whether either set comes from motor neurons.

To date, the tissue origin of ALS plasma proteins has been inferred from tissue expression databases (15, 16). Dergai et al., for example, reported that CLEC3B and ANTXR2 are most highly expressed in microglia and Schwann cells, respectively (16). In contrast, we tested motor neuron origin directly for each plasma protein using iMNs from patients in the same cohort, although our map is limited to motor neurons and cannot exclude an origin in these or other cell types. This raises two considerations. First, a plasma protein that tracks decline in a neurodegenerative disease does not need to come from the degenerating neurons. The strongest progression markers, CLEC3B, ANTXR2, and ART3, were not expressed or were transcript only in iMNs, and several, including CLEC3B and CRTAC1, have been linked to aging, longevity, and joint degeneration in population studies (35, 36). Their decline in plasma may therefore reflect the systemic consequences of ALS, such as denervation, immobility, weight loss, and hypermetabolism (19) on tissues throughout the body. ART3, which is highly expressed in skeletal muscle (16), was lower in patients and fell further with decline, suggesting that muscle contributes to the progression signal through proteins that fall as well as through proteins that leak. The insulin-like growth factor binding protein (IGFBP6) was also a progression marker, and the related IGFBP2 has been associated with survival in ALS (37). This concerns where the plasma signal of progression comes from and not where the disease begins. Whether degeneration starts in the motor cortex (38) or the distal axon and neuromuscular junction (39) plasma proteins that track decline could reflect the consequences of motor neuron loss for muscle and other tissues. Second, the differential plasma proteins and the progression markers reflect different processes. Muscle proteins such as CA3, TNNI2, and MYL11 were the most elevated in patients but did not change with the rate of decline, consistent with ongoing leak from denervated muscle that is present throughout the disease (29, 40). In contrast, the progression markers mostly fell as patients declined. Plasma levels also depend on how a protein is released and not only on its expression, as shown for FGF23, which is increased in ALS muscle but not in plasma (41). Plasma proteins chosen for their difference from controls are therefore not necessarily suited to monitoring progression.

Unexpectedly, the SomaScan NEFL aptamer did not differ between patients and controls and agreed poorly with NfL measured by immunoassay at the same visits. NEFL was measured in plasma and NfL in serum, but NfL levels in the two differ only slightly (42, 43), which cannot account for the low correlation. The SomaScan NEFL aptamer has also shown no agreement with immunoassay NfL in plasma (44), whereas it agrees closely with immunoassay in CSF (45) where NfL is far more abundant. These results suggest that the aptamer does not reliably measure NfL at the concentrations found in blood, and NEFL results from SomaScan plasma data should be treated with caution. This is a limitation of a single aptamer and not of the platform broadly, as the progression markers identified on SomaScan replicated in mass spectrometry in Target ALS. Measured by immunoassay, baseline NfL was strongly prognostic, consistent with previous studies (9, 10, 12). In contrast, change in NfL over time was only weakly related to the rate of decline, even after correction for the reliability of the slope estimates. This is consistent with the relative stability of NfL within patients (9, 10) and suggests that NfL largely reflects each patient's overall rate of neuroaxonal loss and not the decline in function as it accumulates. The exception was patients with low baseline NfL, in whom change in NfL did track decline.

Our findings have direct implications for clinical trials and patient care. NfL is already used to stratify patients and as a pharmacodynamic endpoint (13, 14), but our results suggest that change in NfL is a poor measure of whether functional decline is slowing in most patients. Change in the progression markers tracked decline irrespective of baseline NfL and explained decline beyond it. This supports a complementary approach in which baseline NfL is used to stratify patients at enrolment and a panel of systemic plasma proteins is used to monitor decline during follow-up. The replication of progression markers on mass spectrometry, including CLEC3B and ART3 individually, suggests that a panel would not be restricted to a single platform. Plasma proteins and ALSFRS-R were measured over the same period, so our analyses show that the progression markers track decline as it occurs and not that they predict future decline. Whether they respond to treatment, however, remains to be tested in trial samples.

The progression markers did not track decline in the fastest progressing patients. This was not explained by shorter follow-up or by samples collected close to death and extended to every ALSFRS-R subdomain. Change in NfL similarly failed to track decline in patients with the highest baseline NfL, who overlapped with the fast progressors. Those patients could be recognized at enrolment by a short symptom duration and high baseline NfL and included about half of the C9orf72 expansion carriers. We interpret this not as a limitation of the markers but as evidence that the process driving decline in the fastest progressors is not reflected in change in either systemic or neuronal blood markers. The retained association with the decline in vital capacity and the loss of BMI suggests that respiratory and metabolic change in these patients may still be captured in plasma, whereas the rapid loss of limb and bulbar function is not. Proteomic differences between fast and slow progressors in longitudinal CSF (21) and changes in circulating immune cells (18) have been linked to rapid progression, so markers of decline in these patients may need to be tested in CSF or cells.

Trials that monitor all patients with the same blood biomarkers may therefore be unable to detect a treatment effect in fast progressors. Cohorts with denser sampling earlier in the disease will be needed to identify markers of their decline.

Several further limitations should be considered. First, iMNs are immature relative to adult spinal motor neurons and their expression is influenced by differentiation and line effects (46, 47). Expression in iMNs may therefore differ from that in adult motor neurons, although iMNs expressed all of the canonical motor neuron proteins we tested. Second, the progression markers were identified on SomaScan and only 16 were measured in mass spectrometry in Target ALS, which also lacked visit dates and was too small to compare fast and slow progressors. The inability to track fast progressors therefore rests on a single cohort and requires replication. Third, patients who progress slowly are more likely to enroll later in their disease, which may contribute to the longer symptom duration of the slowest third.

Overall, we identify plasma proteins whose within-patient change tracks the rate of functional decline in ALS, replicate them in an independent cohort, and show using patient iMNs that they originate outside motor neurons. Change in these systemic proteins tracked decline across the range of baseline NfL, whereas change in NfL did not. This positions baseline NfL for prognosis and stratification and systemic plasma proteins for monitoring, an approach that can be applied directly to the design of clinical trials. We also identify the fastest progressing patients as a group whose decline is tracked by neither, highlighting the need for precision biomarker studies designed around these patients.

Materials and Methods

Study design

The objective of this study was to identify plasma proteins whose within-patient change tracks the rate of functional decline in ALS, to test whether they originate from motor neurons, and to compare them with serum NfL. We used all participants available in the Answer ALS and Target ALS public data releases who met the data requirements of each analysis. As the data were generated previously (22) (23) (24) there was no further randomization or blinding.

Cohorts

Answer ALS recruited individuals with sporadic and familial ALS and age-matched neurologically unimpaired controls across eight US neuromuscular centers (22). Sex was selfreported (Table S1). Functional impairment was assessed at each visit using the ALSFRS-R total score (2). Time was defined as years since screening. Disease duration was calculated as the difference between age at first peripheral blood mononuclear cell (PBMC) collection and age at symptom onset. The Target ALS Global Natural History Study is a multi-center longitudinal cohort in which plasma was profiled by TMT mass spectrometry and Olink (Table S5) (24). Visit dates were not available in the clinical release, so time was represented by visit number. All participants provided written informed consent, and study procedures were approved by the institutional review boards of each participating site and adhered to the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki (22, 24). No separate ethics approval was required as this study used publicly available data.

Plasma proteomics and serum NfL

Plasma was profiled using the SomaScan v4.1 assay, which measures approximately 7,500 aptamers using slow off-rate modified aptamers (48). Data were normalized by SomaLogic using adaptive normalization by maximum likelihood, and relative fluorescent units (RFU) were log 2 -transformed. The 7,550 aptamers with an annotated UniProt accession were analyzed separately and identified by their SomaScan sequence identifier. The baseline sample was each participant's earliest sample. Serum NfL was measured by Answer ALS on the Siemens Atellica immunoassay platform, reported in pg/mL, and log 2 -transformed, giving 1,655 draws from 740 patients with ALS.

Motor neuron expression map

iPSCs were generated from patient PBMCs and differentiated into iMNs, which were profiled on day 32 by RNA-sequencing, label-free mass spectrometry, and ATAC-sequencing (22, 23). Each aptamer was mapped from its UniProt accession to a gene. A plasma protein was considered detected at the transcript level if its gene had five or more counts in at least 20% of iMN lines and a mean variance-stabilized expression above the 10 th percentile across all genes. It was detected at the protein level if it was quantified in at least 50% of iMN lines in the matrix before batch correction and imputation. Its promoter was considered accessible if any ATAC-sequencing peak within 2 kb of its transcription start site had more than five counts in at least 20% of lines. Plasma proteins were assigned to the five classes of the map from these calls, with expressed plasma proteins classed as promoter-unconfirmed when no accessible promoter peak was identified. A grounding score from 0 to 3 was assigned to each plasma protein as the number of layers (transcript, protein, and accessible promoter) with supporting evidence in iMNs. Processing and validation are described in the Supplementary Methods.

Differential plasma proteins

Differences in baseline plasma protein levels between patients with ALS and controls were assessed using linear models with empirical Bayes moderation in 'limma' (49), adjusting for sex and age. Plasma proteins with a Benjamini-Hochberg (50) FDR below 0.05 were considered differential plasma proteins. Within patients, each differential plasma protein was related to the baseline ALSFRS-R score and to disease duration by Pearson correlation, with FDR controlled across the 77 proteins for each.

Longitudinal analyses

Within-patient change in plasma proteins was related to the rate of functional decline using a two-stage design (51, 52). In the first stage, each patient's rate of decline was estimated from all dated ALSFRS-R scores in patients with two or more assessments (n = 663) using a linear mixed-effects model in 'lme4' with a fixed effect of time and participantspecific random intercepts and slopes, fit by restricted maximum likelihood (53). Each patient's rate of decline was taken as the best linear unbiased predictor (BLUP) of their slope (54). Each patient's rate of change in each plasma protein was estimated in the same way in patients with two or more dated draws and an ALSFRS-R slope (n = 229), and an aptamer was tested only if at least 20 patients contributed two or more measurements. In the second stage, each patient's protein slope was related to their ALSFRS-R slope by Pearson correlation, with FDR controlled across the 7,550 aptamers. Aptamers with an FDR below 0.05 were considered progression markers. ALSFRS-R slopes are negative in decline, so a positive correlation indicates that faster decline was accompanied by a faster fall in plasma level. The two-stage design was compared with alternative methods by simulation. Cohorts of 229 patients were simulated from the visit schedules, variance components, and dropout estimated in Answer ALS, each with 1,000 plasma proteins of which five tracked decline, and the methods were compared on power and FDR. The methods were then compared in the cohort on the number of aptamers identified and their replication between random halves (Fig. S1 to S3; Supplementary Methods).

Motor neuron expression and progression tracking

Progression tracking was defined as the absolute correlation between protein slope and ALSFRS-R slope. For the 7,175 aptamers that mapped to an annotated gene, tracking was regressed on grounding score, first without adjustment and then with adjustment for each aptamer's mean baseline signal and its coefficient of variation. The adjusted coefficient was compared against a null distribution from 2,000 permutations of grounding score across aptamers. Enrichment of map classes among the differential plasma proteins and progression markers was assessed against the panel using Fisher's exact test. Route to plasma and tissue distribution were assessed using concordR (v0.2.0) (30) as described in the Supplementary Methods.

NEFL and NfL

The NEFL aptamer (SomaScan sequence identifier 10082-251) was examined in the slope design (n = 229) and in a baseline design in which ALSFRS-R slope was regressed on baseline NEFL (n = 242), with CLEC3B and ANTXR2 as positive controls. Agreement between NEFL and NfL was assessed by Pearson correlation in draws in which both were measured at the same visit. NfL was then examined in the same two designs. The observed correlation between NfL slope and ALSFRS-R slope was corrected for the reliability of the two slope estimates (55). Regression to the mean was tested using NfL slopes re-estimated from follow-up draws alone, as described in the Supplementary Methods.

Composite score and comparison with NfL

The composite score was calculated by standardizing each marker slope across patients, multiplying it by the sign of the marker's correlation with ALSFRS-R slope, and averaging across the 72 progression markers. The composite was also cross-fitted by were randomly dividing patients into two halves, selecting the 72 aptamers most strongly correlated with ALSFRS-R slope in one half, and scoring the composite in the other using the signs from the first. This was done in both directions and repeated 100 times, and each patient's composite was averaged across repeats. For comparison, each patient's NfL slope was estimated by regressing log 2 NfL on time and sign-reversed, so that a positive correlation indicates that change tracks decline. The associations of the cross-fitted composite and of NfL slope with ALSFRS-R slope were compared using Pearson correlation, and their difference was tested with 2,000 paired bootstrap resamples. The contribution of the composite beyond NfL was assessed by comparing linear models of ALSFRS-R slope on baseline NfL and NfL slope with and without the composite using an F test. The comparison was then repeated after dividing patients into three groups of equal size by their baseline NfL level (low, intermediate, and high).

Tracking across rates of decline

Patients were divided into thirds of equal size by their ALSFRS-R slope. Within each third, the composite was regressed on ALSFRS-R slope, so that patients were grouped on the predictor and not on the outcome, and the difference between the fastest and slowest thirds was tested by the interaction between ALSFRS-R slope and third. Robustness analyses and clinical comparisons between thirds are described in the Supplementary Methods.

Replication in Target ALS

Differences between patients with ALS and controls were assessed in 'limma' with adjustment for sex and age, and for TMT set on mass spectrometry. Proteins were matched to Answer ALS by gene symbol. Concordance was assessed as the proportion changed in the same direction, tested against 50% with a two-sided binomial test, and by Pearson correlation of effect sizes. For progression, ALSFRS-R slopes (n = 133) and protein slopes (n = 50) were estimated using the same mixed-effects models. Concordance with the Answer ALS progression markers was assessed in the same way. A composite of the progression markers was then calculated with each marker's direction fixed from Answer ALS, so that no marker was selected in Target ALS, and was related to ALSFRS-R slope by Pearson correlation with a one-sided permutation p-value. This was compared with 1,000 composites of the same number of randomly selected non-marker proteins.

Statistical analyses

Bootstrap 95% CIs were calculated from 2,000 resamples. All analyses were done in R (v4.5.1) using 'dplyr', 'tidyr', 'lme4', 'lmerTest', 'limma', 'DESeq2', 'edgeR', 'GenomicRanges', 'ChIPseeker', 'TxDb.Hsapiens.UCSC.hg38.knownGene', 'org.Hs.eg.db', 'AnnotationDbi', and 'concordR'.

For up-to-date information on the study, visit https://dataportal.answerals.org. Data was also sourced from the Target ALS Global Natural History Study. More information on the study can be found at the Target ALS Data Engine: https://targetals.org/research/target-als-data-engine/.

proteomics, serum NfL, and iMN RNA-sequencing, mass spectrometry, and ATAC- sequencing, are available to researchers on application through the Answer ALS Data Portal (https://dataportal.answerals.org; AALS-01184). The Target ALS Global Natural History Study clinical data and plasma mass spectrometry and Olink data are available on application through the Target ALS Data Engine (https://targetals.org/research/target-als-data-engine/). No new data or materials were generated in this study. All results supporting the findings are provided in the paper and the Supplementary Materials. The code and results for all analyses and figures are publicly available at https://github.com/Art83/als_long. The code for the simulations comparing the two-stage design with alternative methods is publicly available at https://github.com/Art83/als_sim.
